utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon to everybody, in particular those assisting us before and behind the scenes. Mr. Bonabello, would you be so kind to call the case on behalf of the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is case number IT-01-42-A, the Prosecutor versus Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I have the appearances, please. The Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon to the Defence and the other court personnel. Helen Brady appearing on behalf of the Prosecution together with Mr. Xavier Tracol, and our case manager Ms. Victoria McCreath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Vladimir Petrovic. I'm co-counsel for the accused, General Pavle Strugar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Strugar, may I ask you: Can you hear me and follow the proceed information a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you have any complaints about the conditions in the United Nations Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then are there in particular new health problems apart from those general issues we have to discuss later in the framework of this Status Conference or in other environment foreseen in the Rules?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The intensity of my pains is a bit more frequent, especially when walking. Other than that, I have no new complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated again. Please, the parties may correct me if I'm wrong, I take it that the filing of the appeal briefs, the responses, and replies is now completed. May I ask are there any objections as to the lengths of the briefs or its contents, in particular anything you have identified that should be treated confidentially?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is only one matter I wish to raise about the Defence reply brief, and we do notice that it's somewhat oversized by approximately one and a half pages, but the Prosecution doesn't take issue and doesn't object to the filing in that form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- yes. As a kind of give and take, let my address: Also at the same time there was an addendum to the book of authorities for Prosecution appeal brief dated 12 July 2005, not accompanied by any motion. Does the Defence have any objections that we take this without any further ado as part of the book of authorities for Prosecution appeal brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has no objection to including it in the material referred to by the Prosecution in their appeal brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it's now clear what we have before us. You may be a little bit surprised, but in order to be on the safe side I want to go through the notice of appeal presented by the Defence, alleged error by alleged error, from 1 to 100, that you we are abundantly clear what we have before us. So would you therefore please be so kind and take this notice of appeal. I can see both parties are now in possession of this document. The confusion might emanate from the fact that, for example, under paragraph 9 you have alleged error number 1. And I will from now on refer only to the alleged error. Please correct me immediately when I'm wrong or if there is any doubt. Error 1, alleged error 1, withdrawn. 2, withdrawn. 3 upheld, 4 upheld, 5 upheld, 6 upheld, 7 upheld, 8 upheld, 9 upheld, 10 upheld, 11 upheld, 12 upheld, 13 withdrawn, 14 withdrawn, 15 withdrawn, 16 withdrawn, 17 withdrawn, 26 upheld [sic], 19 upheld, 20 upheld, 21 upheld, 22 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. Could we please go back to the transcript. I think that the transcript that I have in front of me says 26 upheld and it should have been 18 upheld. This seems to be an error, especially in view of the order that you read the errors in. So could we please go back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If it could be corrected. That's line -- page 3, line 19, 26 should be replaced by "18 upheld." Mr. Registrar, I take it that this will be corrected. So we can take it that it will be corrected. We came to 22, error 22, and there it should read "withdrawn" instead of "upheld." 23 withdrawn, 24 upheld, 25 upheld, 26 upheld, 27 upheld, 28 upheld, 29 upheld, 30 upheld, 31 upheld, 32 upheld, 33 withdrawn, 34 upheld, 35 upheld, 36 upheld, 37 upheld, 38 withdrawn, 39 withdrawn, 40 upheld, 41 withdrawn, 42 withdrawn, 43 withdrawn, 44 upheld, 45 upheld, 46 upheld, 47 withdrawn, 48 withdrawn, 49 upheld, 50 withdrawn, 51 withdrawn, 52 withdrawn, 53 withdrawn, 54 upheld, 55 upheld, 56 withdrawn, 57 withdrawn, 58 withdrawn, 59 withdrawn, 60 withdrawn, 61 withdrawn, 62 withdrawn, 63 withdrawn, 72 withdrawn, 73 -- oh, sorry. I have to restart. I was again confused by the paragraph and the error number. Could we please start again with 64. 64 is upheld, 65 withdrawn, 66 withdrawn, 67 withdrawn, 68 withdrawn, 69 withdrawn, 70 withdrawn, 71 withdrawn, 72 withdrawn, 73 withdrawn, 74 upheld, 75 withdrawn, 76 withdrawn, 77 upheld, 78 withdrawn, 79 upheld, 80 upheld, 81 withdrawn, 82 withdrawn, 83 upheld, 84 upheld, 85 upheld, 86 upheld, 87 upheld, 88 upheld, 89 upheld, 90 upheld, 91 upheld, 92 withdrawn, 93 upheld, 94 upheld, 95 upheld, 96 upheld, 97 upheld, 98 upheld, 99 upheld, and finally 100 upheld. Is this correct? I see a nodding from both sides. Then the question to both parties: Can we agree that we can and should use the numbers allocated to the reasons of appeal in this notice of appeal and not, which would no doubt be the alternative, renumber the reasons in your appeal brief which I'm afraid could create some confusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This would be also suitable to the Prosecution. I noticed the Defence appeal brief has essentially five grounds, and so in effect the grounds in the notice of appeal are split up among these five, but I think for ease of reference we could certainly use the ones in the notice of appeal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I take it as an agreed fact that we refer to these numbers allocated to the reasons of appeal in the initial notice of appeal. Are there any problems related to disclosure, any complaints by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is my duty to inform you that from the minute the hearings were concluded in this trial there were no further -- there was no further disclosure from the Prosecution on any grounds. Therefore, I can't really state our position as there was no disclosure as such. Now, as to whether there was any material that should have about disclosed to us in accordance with the Rules I really can't say. I believe that if there was such material the Defence would have received Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it. However, we have not received anything, so I believe that things are in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear the Prosecution on this. Is there any search done or was there any search done in the past?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: You were, we are continuing with our disclosure obligations. To date nothing that is come to light that falls within our obligations under Rule 68(i) and if and when material comes to light we'll of course disclose to the Defence accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I take that we continue you with the, one might call it old-fashioned system and not with the electronic disclosure system in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are using the EDS system in this case and our searches are across material which is not on the EDS system. Your Honour, to do otherwise would create the problems that were in the -- were inherent in the old system. So our disclosure searches proceed on the basis that we search across non-EDS material, and if we come across material which needs to be disclosed according to our obligation, we will of course disclose. But in terms of material which is on the EDS, the Defence, I understand, has access to the EDS and will be able to utilise the search terms that he has at hand to access material in the EDS. We think that this is the most efficient way forward in handling disclosure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. But to come back to this question, the EDS in general, of course it's accessible for the Defence, but you have no special case related, let's call it database for this concrete case where the Defence would have access in an electronic way to those documents and the Defence would be on the permanent obligation to look up whether something has become new in this concrete case file, to put it this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: We can certainly alert the Defence to new indices and give a general description of the documents that have been placed on the EDS since the dates of the hearing. To my knowledge, and I would have to check this, there may be two indices that have been placed on since this matter -- since the hearing. Those two indices are probably not pertaining to the actual crime scene to the crime base that's of relevance to this accused. But if there are indices then the Prosecution will certainly -- specific indices, the Prosecution will certainly notify the Defence so that they're under -- well, basically know where to look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I take it that the Defence will continue interpreting Rule 68 to that end, that whenever something specific for the concrete case which normally, as it was in the past, would -- there would be the need that you have to disclose under Rule 68 this material you would alert the Defence on this in particular. So you are satisfied with this solution or you have problems with the access to the electronic disclosure system, which I know can be difficult to access from abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we don't have any problems accessing the system. To the extent possible, we search everything that could possibly pertain to our client. It should be noted that the EDS system does not have a separate segment pertaining to this accused. Rather, we have to search the general database which makes this process much more complex and longer. However, I would like to thank you for your interpretation of Rule 68. In addition, I would like to add that it would be very useful to the Defence if we could be periodically informed about the new numbers of documents which were included in the EDS so that we could shorten the time we need to search the EDS and to avoid any duplication of searches. If we could be provided information about the new documents included into the system, that would be very useful because that would mean that we do not have to duplicate the search, to redo something that has been done in the past. I don't know whether this is feasible, whether we can address our colleagues in the Prosecution directly regarding this, or perhaps we should turn to the EDS administration personnel. I don't know. If you have any advice concerning this, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me ask Prosecution. Wouldn't it be the best way to deal with this that whenever a document pertaining to not only the concrete crime site but also to the accused that you would immediately inform the Defence, this being part of your disclosure obligation?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the collections of documents are seized, of course we're talking about extremely large volumes of documents which take a while to be scanned and to be put onto the EDS. Within -- so it's not as if the Prosecution can immediately identify that there is one document within a collection of 300.000, let's say, that would be of relevance to this case. I think that perhaps the best solution to this is that we will continue abide by our Rule 68(i) and if matters which fall within that -- come within our knowledge we will disclose. In the meantime, what we can do is identify what collections, relevant collections have come in and I think from the description and where the documents were seized from and what they generally are about, I think from that the Defence will be able to clearly see whether this is a matter which they need to apply their search criteria to. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: This, we believe, is probably the best way forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. I can agree with this provided that we take into account that, in fact, opposed to other cases where we have not only the general EDS system but a case-related separate setting of documents accessible for the Defence, that when we continue a case on appeal that we should continue in the, let's call it again, old-fashioned way, and I think the burden to disclose this material is still with the Prosecutor. And I think it's -- it fits best in the rationale and the spirit behind Rule 68 that we continue with this. It will be no doubt only a limited number of relevant documents falling into the scope of Rule 68(i). I think we can agree on this and -- or should there be any problems, please alert me immediately that we can resolve this matter. This brings me to the next question -- yes, sorry, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes. If I could just add to that that the Prosecution and perhaps if we go back to Rule 68(ii), we can make available to the Defence in electronic form the collections of relevant material which we have by placing it on EDS, and we can make a case-specific, Strugar-specific folder on the EDS so that the Defence can get access to that. But -- and then of course we can file with our Rule 68 (i) obligations to -- disclose material within our actual knowledge falls within 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think this would be helpful for one of the parties. You would have additional workload to provide such a new folder, and then as there is -- this electronic disclosure system is still flawed, no doubt, and you can't see when accessing these documents what is inside. You have to open all the documents because only the number of the documents is revealed on the screen, and therefore I think the easiest way for both parties is whenever you come across something that could fall under the scope of Rule 68(i), then you should alert the other party and not start a new folder for this case where I think most of the documents have already been admitted into evidence and the likelihood that there is fundamental new document as all the archives have been opened now seems to be limited. So I would really appreciate if you could avoid entering in a new area of disclosure in this case but still continue under -- let's call it under the old Rules. Could you live with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, we will always provide to the Defence that which falls within Rule 68(i), which comes within our actual knowledge. We're talking about documents which may be of more tangential relevance to the case, and there it actually, I think, can speed the process by making sure that the Defence knows which indices the Defence is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to look into. Otherwise, the Prosecution, under the old fashioned system as you quite rightly referred to it, is in the position that you're searching across the entirety of the evidence collection and then having to review it, each piece individually, and this is the system that I understand the Prosecution's position is, we've moved away from by the EDS system. So it's hard for me to agree to Your Honour's suggestion in light of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In fact, this would be a kind of compromise not open a new folder for the specific purposes of the case before us but to alert the Defence when there is a new or there are new indices pertaining to the concrete case before us, and then it would be for the Defence, and there is also some advantage for the Defence to label the documents itself whether they tend to be exculpatory or not. So if you can agree on this basis, I think this would be an excellent solution that you alert on indices and the Defence would then open these indices and look into the documents contained in this collection. Would this be acceptable for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, it would be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this would be acceptable to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask already now is there any intention of one or both parties to file a motion for the admission of additional evidence under Rule 115?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Not at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as we notified you at the previous Status Conference, not at present. Our work, however, and our efforts to find a highly relevant document which would meet the criteria for additional evidence is ongoing. So should such a document turn up, we will make the appropriate submission. However, at present we do not have such a document in our possession. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. Now let's come to a more serious point, and maybe from the point of view of Mr. Strugar, the most serious one, and that is the question of the health of Mr. Strugar. We all got, I take it, the fundamental documents pertaining to Mr. Strugar's health, but we have not yet got any assessment of this data and what would be the indication, what would be the necessary measures to be taken to undergo an operation or whatsoever. But I really don't believe that it's appropriate to go into the details of this in the framework of a Status Conference. I think it was right from the Defence to ask for not discussing this matter today before academics have given an assessment and come to the conclusion what has to be done. So therefore, in my opinion, it would be more than appropriate to have a 65 ter (I) Conference as soon as possible when you have an assessment. And it's also for the Prosecution. I would invite both parties, before we have such a 65 ter (I) meeting to discuss these matters. And only to tell you in terms of time what would -- is feasible in the concrete case and what is not, normally one could say the stage of filings is completed. Now we would be ready for the appeals hearing. However, I just took the Appeals Chamber summary 2005 of 26 August 2005, and there I unfortunately found out that based on the criteria we used in the past that the first incoming appeal will be heard first. We, with our case, are number 13 or 14, depending on how you count in this -- in this order, which means that there is no substantial likelihood that the case can be heard this year. About next year, that is the Appeals Chamber will have to convene and to give priorities to some cases. But I would really appreciate if you could also with the light -- in view of this order of cases that we can discuss when, in case it's necessary, that Mr. Strugar undergoes an operation that we can find the appropriate time, the appropriate venue, and -- because it's a very intimate question, it should be done in the framework of such a Rule 65 ter meeting. May I ask the Defence, when would you be able to come up an assessment of all the data we have also now in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the Defence would be able to make this assessment by the end of September, that is, within the next two or three weeks at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then invite that the parties meet before and we try to have such a meeting in week 40. This would be the first week of October. Are there any obstacles to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution remains happy, of course, to attend a Rule 65 ter (I) Conference. We would ask Your Honour not to hold it in week 40 if -- if convenient, if we could have it the week following. Both myself and Mr. Tracol will be in the argument -- in the appeals hearing of Stakic that week, and so we would, if it's convenient for the Defence and for Your Honour, prefer week 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be the second week of October. I can't see any obstacles to this. Let's be very concrete. What about that very Tuesday in the second week of October? Would it be suitable for both parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's suitable for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then in order to avoid unnecessary filings, I hereby convene a Rule 65 ter (I), 107 meeting, conference, in my office, that is room M149, together with one representative of the Registrar to take minutes from this meeting and then to discuss how to proceed in this case and, in particular, all the medical aspects but not limited to this. But beforehand, as we are in a party-driven system, let's me again invite both parties to discuss the possible avenues to be taken proprio motu and then it would facilitate and speed up this specific conference. Finally, are there any other issues to be raised by the parties? The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we will meet, then, in week 41. And, Mr. Strugar, I indeed do hope that your health does not deteriorate, but I think you also find it reasonable first to discuss in detail your health situation based on real facts and then to decide how to continue best, and I think no doubt your counsel will discuss these problems with you. We will all try to do our very best that your health condition is not affected by the fact that unfortunately we can't hear the appeal immediately. Thank you once again to everybody. The trial stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: at 3.03 p.m.
